correctness.rationale: The precise transform normalization follows by Fourier inversion and spherical orthogonality. DLMF 10.22.57 gives the exact Bessel-square moment; Debye asymptotics and matched mass establish the scaled spectral law; Potter bounds and shifted moments control noncompact tails. On compact scaled intervals the oscillating phases have either nonzero first or nonzero second derivative, so fixed-frequency spectral oscillations vanish. The Wendland constants and endpoint cosine are substituted directly from the primary source. Exact moments and finite oscillatory examples were independently checked with the embedded script; those tests do not prove the theorem.

originality.rationale: The new result is the general exact asymptotic for arbitrary positive slowly varying envelopes and finitely many fixed, nonvanishing oscillatory spectral terms, not the Wendland special-case formula already asserted in 2021. Explicit formula comparison with the 2023 conjecture and with classical Bessel moments and earlier rate-only restriction bounds does not yield an implication covering this general theorem; a residual unindexed classical transfer theorem is possible.
residual_risks: The 2021 arXiv v1 asserts even-dimensional Wendland asymptotics; no novelty or priority is claimed for that expression alone.
A classical large-order Bessel-square Abelian theorem equivalent to the general result may exist outside the inspected sources.
Full text of Le Gia–Sloan–Wendland (2010) and Ridenhour–Soni (1974) was not accessible; conclusions about them are limited to available abstract and cited descriptions.

value.rationale: Spherical spectra of radial positive-definite kernels govern exact Sobolev norm equivalences and covariance simulations. The theorem recovers a precise spectral constant despite persistent Euclidean spectral oscillations of order one, a nonstandard boundary behavior in generalized Wendland functions. It also proves the even-dimensional asymptotic explicitly posed as Conjecture 5.10 in the 2023 publication. The general theorem accommodates infinitely many slowly varying choices and is not a parameter substitution.
